newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: COFFEE-Colombia puts bad coffee year behind it.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE-Colombia puts bad coffee year behind it.

text.p: Colombia has ended its 1995-1996 coffee year, a period that industry officials are happy to put behind them since it was the worst since the International Coffee Agreement collapsed in 1989.

But the 1996-97 coffee year that began Tuesday comes against a backdrop of mounting woes, including an escalation in leftist guerrilla activity in the central coffee- growing region. And apart from the possibility of less rain during the flowering period, there appears to be little reason to think that it will be any better than the previous year.

"The most troublesome thing are the social problems the region is facing," Alberto Jaramillo, head of the Coffee Growers Committee in central Caldas province, told the domestic news agency Colprensa, referring to guerrilla unrest.

He added that the presence of rebel groups in most of the municipalities of Caldas had led to a "breakdown in public security" -- a complaint that has been heard across much of the country since its two top rebel groups went on a nationwide offensive over the past month.

President Ernesto Samper announced Tuesday that the security situation had been brought fully under control by the military, but there were continuing reports of guerrilla attacks and highway blockades in parts of the country.

Official figures are not in yet for the 1995-1996 coffee year, but industry sources say production is expected to total no more than 12.6 million 60-kilo bags, down from 13 million in the previous coffee year.

The drop has been attributed to unusually heavy rains during the flowering period beginning in December and to soaring production costs including those associated with fighting the berry borer -- a plague that threatens to ravish trees across the country.

Coupled with low market prices for coffee, the rise in production costs -- much of it stemming from Colombia's notoriously high interest rates -- cost growers nearly $100 million during the last coffee year in Caldas alone, according to Fabio Trujillo, head of the independent Unidad Cafetera Nacional.

According to the National Coffee Growers Federation, Colombia's green coffee production costs totalled $0.94 per pound in 1995, putting the country at a competitive disadvantage with growers like Costa Rica where production costs last year totalled no more than $0.77 per pound.

The biggest immediate concern for Colombia's coffee sector is the country's buoyant peso currency, however, which has strengthened considerably since early June when it was trading at more than 1,074 to the dollar. It rose in trading Wednesday to a nine-month high of 1,017.25.

The trend toward a stronger peso makes Colombian goods more expensive abroad, and means that exporters get less pesos from their foreign exchange revenues. The coffee industry is among the hardest hit by the appreciation, since it imports are dwarfed by those of other industries and it has little need for cheap dollars.
"We're reaching some really unsustainable levels," Roberto Pizarro, head of the Coffee Growers Committee in southwest Valle province said of the exchange rate Wednesday.

According to the National Coffee Growers Federation, the stronger peso, which is rising on the back of Colombia's increasing oil income, has cost Colombia more than $2.8 billion in coffee export revenues over the past six years.
Exporters and even President Samper have called for a devaluation of the peso to help breathe new life into coffee and other industries.
But the central bank, which likes a strong currency as a buffer against inflation, has insisted that it has no intention of undercutting the peso artifically.
